$comment: One entry per fixture. Read by both the TypeScript and Rust test suites — see ../README.md.
EVERY FIELD IS MEASURED. Nothing here is written from theory: two earlier attempts to predict
importer behaviour were wrong, so the fields waited for B-007 milestone 1 to run.
IMPORT SIDE (pgn-reader, measured at milestone 1): `importOutcome` is `imports` or `refused` —
17 and 1 respectively. `importTags` and `importTokens` are what the parser handed back, and they
are the interesting numbers: a token count below the file's own is pgn-reader DROPPING tokens it
IMPORTER SIDE (measured at milestone 2): `importedTags` is how many tags survive the importer's
first-one-wins map. It differs from `importTags` on exactly one fixture, and that difference IS
the duplicate-tag decision — the parser reports every repeat, choosing between them is ours.
DISPLAY SIDE (chessops, measured at B-099): `plies` and `truncatedAtPly`.
THE TWO SIDES DISAGREE, AND THE DISAGREEMENTS ARE THE POINT. Same file, different results, no
complaint from either library — see ADR-0009's Accepted risks table.
`rule` cites the ADR-0009 rule a fixture illustrates. The notes carry the findings.

fixtures.note: The negative control: conforms in every respect. A corpus that only held rejections would be passed by an importer that refuses everything.

**Measured: the two sides ship different ply counts for this game, and that is by design.** `pgn-reader` accepts all nine tokens, because it does not check legality; chessops refuses `4. Qg7` — well-formed SAN, illegal in the position — so `mainline.ts` truncates at 6. So the library table would say nine plies while the board stops at six. **Accepted**: the alternative is a legality walk over every imported game to make a column agree with a viewer, which is the validation ADR-0009 declines. Two further legal-looking moves follow the illegal one deliberately, so a reader that skipped rather than stopped would report the wrong ply.

**The one fixture `pgn-reader` refuses, and the libraries could not disagree more.** MEASURED both sides: pgn-reader stops with `unterminated comment` and yields no game at all, while chessops reads it as a complete success — the unclosed `{` swallows moves 3 and 4 and the termination marker, and `truncatedAtPly` is null. So this game never imports, and if it somehow did, the display would show three plies of a six-ply game and say nothing. An earlier version of this note claimed the silence was on *both* sides; that was written before the Rust side was measured, and it was wrong.

**A clean divergence, measured on both sides.** chessops turns this into TWO games: the unclosed quote in [Event "...] runs on to the next quote, consuming the following tag lines, and the leftover movetext becomes a separate game with default headers — hence `plies: 0` for the first. `pgn-reader` recovers instead: ONE game, all seven roster tags correct, four tokens. Same bytes, different game count, no complaint from either. Consequence worth keeping: **a game's index within a file is not a stable identifier**, so an error must carry identifying header text rather than lean on the index.

**Measured on both sides, and the Rust side is better — which retired an accepted risk.** chessops FILLS IN the five absent roster tags with defaults (Event becomes "?", Result "*"), so its header map always holds seven and a missing tag is indistinguishable from a literal "?". `pgn-reader` reports the two tags that actually exist. So "telling them apart needs byte inspection we are not doing" was true of chessops and false of the importer: **the parser simply tells the truth, for free.**

**Measured on both sides, and they differ.** `Result` appears twice (1-0 then 0-1) and `Date` twice. chessops collapses to seven tags, keeping the FIRST. `pgn-reader` hands back all nine in file order, duplicates included. So this is not a validation question at all — **the importer has to choose**, and choosing is a documented decision rather than a check. First-one-wins matches chessops and keeps the two sides consistent, which is the only reason to prefer it.

An ACCEPTED RISK, and the one question milestone 1 did **not** answer. MEASURED for chessops: the tag reads [Result "1-0"], the movetext ends 0-1, and chessops reports 0-1 — the termination marker silently overwrites the header. On the Rust side the probe printed tag *names* only, so which value `pgn-reader` yields is still unknown; `Visitor::outcome()` reports the marker separately from the tag, so the importer will have both and must pick. **Pick the tag, and prefer consistency with chessops if they conflict** — but measure it at milestone 2 rather than assuming.

A complete roster and no movetext. Nothing refuses it, so it becomes a row with no moves. An earlier draft of ADR-0009 added a zero-moves rule to reject this and the one below; the owner's correction was that this is still our validation wearing a smaller hat. It is also not obviously wrong — a scheduled-but-unplayed game legitimately looks like this.

A PNG signature plus random bytes, named .pgn — an ACCEPTED RISK, and measured differently on each side. `pgn-reader` returns one game with **zero tags and zero tokens**; chessops returns one game with seven *fabricated* default headers. Either way **'the parser returned a game' is not evidence that a game exists** — but the Rust row is at least visibly empty, since every hot field derives from tags there are none of. Rejecting it means a rule of ours; if the junk row ever becomes annoying, the targeted fix is one line plus this fixture.

The one deliberate tolerance in ADR-0009 — compliance rather than permissiveness, because the PGN specification names ISO 8859-1 while modern exporters emit UTF-8 and declare nothing. Try UTF-8, fall back to Latin-1: two lines, and rejecting this file would mean rejecting a conforming one. Without the fallback the moves parse perfectly and the accented player names come back as U+FFFD, so the game looks fine and the people in it are quietly corrupted (B-058).

**THE MOST IMPORTANT FIXTURE IN THE CORPUS. Both libraries silently produce a different wrong game, and they are not the same wrong game.** File: `e4 e5 Sf3 Sc6 Lb5 a6`. chessops REWRITES the unrecognised piece letter — `Sf3` becomes the legal pawn move `f3` — and truncates later at `Lb5`, giving `e4 e5 f3 c6`. `pgn-reader` DROPS the tokens it cannot parse entirely, giving `e4 e5 a6`, in which black's `a6` has become white's third move. **Neither reports anything.** So a German-notation file imports with a ply count of 3, displays as a four-ply game that was never played, and the two numbers disagree — all silently. This is ADR-0009's central accepted risk, and it is accepted knowingly: detecting it means the notation-language scan of ADR-0008 rule 4, rejected as B-098. The guard is that chess.com and lichess emit English SAN. **Owner's decision (session 5): assume all PGN input is English SAN.** Recorded as a KNOWN ISSUE in **B-115** and flagged for better error handling in a later release — where the mechanism should be a token-count comparison (the parser dropped something) rather than language detection (which language).

The same double failure through a different convention: file `e4 e5 Cf3 Cc6 Fb5 a6`, chessops gives `e4 e5 f3 c6`, `pgn-reader` gives `e4 e5 a6`. Two fixtures rather than one because the conventions use different letters, and because a single example invites a special case for one language. Same known issue: **B-115**.

What strictness bought, in one file. White has Ke1 and Ra1, both able to reach d1, so `Rd1` is a legal rook move in English and a legal KING move in French; legality cannot arbitrate between them. ADR-0008 needed a rule and a heuristic file-wide language scan for this. Under ADR-0009 the question does not arise: the library reads English SAN, plays the rook, and the game imports. B-098 was rejected on the strength of this.

A legal Crazyhouse game. On the display side chessops reads the `Variant` tag, returns a Crazyhouse position and plays `P@e4` as a drop — pocket visible in the FEN. **The importer does not care**: it builds no position, so all eight rule sets are the display's business until the position index arrives. One measurement artefact worth recording so nobody chases it: `pgn-reader` round-trips the drop as `@e4` rather than `P@e4`, which is how `SanPlus` *formats* a pawn drop, not a parse difference. The probe flagged it as ALTERED, which is a false positive in the instrument.

A `Variant` tag naming something neither library implements ("Grand Chess"). MEASURED: `pgn-reader` imports it happily with three tokens, because it builds no position. chessops refuses to build one at all (ERR_VARIANT), surfacing as `truncatedAtPly` 0 — indistinguishable from an unparseable FEN. So an unsupported variant is an import success and a display failure, which is the same shape as the illegal-move fixture.

The quietest failure in the corpus, and both sides are quiet. MEASURED: [Variant "Fischerandom"] silently maps to STANDARD chess in chessops, so a Chess960 game with no FEN derives a mainline that is legal and wrong, reporting nothing; `pgn-reader` imports the four tokens without an opinion. An ACCEPTED RISK, because catching it means checking variant names against a list we maintain. Real Chess960 exports carry SetUp/FEN — and 'normally' is doing the work in that sentence.

Both dedupe fixtures simply import, because there is no dedupe: ADR-0008's content key was removed from the MVP before ADR-0009 removed the rest. Kept as specification for B-022, whenever merging earns a customer. Ten tags, per-move { [%clk] } comments, movetext wrapped across three lines, LF endings.

The same game re-exported: seven tags, clock comments stripped, different wrapping, CRLF endings, marker on its own line. Byte-different in every respect a naive hash would notice, identical in players, event, date, round, result and moves. Importing both produces two rows — the expected MVP behaviour, worth a test so nobody 'fixes' it into a silent merge. Whenever B-022 keys on games, the key must include the variant.
